planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Purple Sensation is one of the darkest and most saturated hyacinths in commerce, its dense spike opening a rich royal-purple that reads nearly plum in low light, carrying the same intensely sweet, powerful fragrance typical of the species. Its bold color makes a dramatic contrast against pale yellow or white hyacinths, early white daffodils, or emerging chartreuse foliage in a mixed spring border. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since the bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for good flowering in subsequent years without repeat chilling.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to very early fall in well-drained soil; like other fall crocus, flowers emerge from bare ground within weeks of planting, with foliage following later.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade. Native to Turkey and the Aegean region, this dainty fall-blooming species produces abundant, pale lilac-blue goblet flowers with a soft violet throat, often opening several blooms per corm in September and October ahead of its grassy foliage. It is one of the easiest and most reliable fall crocus species for naturalizing in a rock garden, gravel bed, or the front of a sunny border, multiplying steadily by offsets and self-seeding where drainage stays sharp through summer dormancy. As a true crocus it has three stamens and slender leaves, distinguishing it from the toxic, superficially similar Colchicum.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this species is among the earliest crocus to flower, often opening in late winter ahead of most other spring bulbs.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in a sunny, sharply drained spot such as a rock garden or the front of a border, planting in fall for bloom in late winter. Native to rocky slopes around Naples in southern Italy, it produces slender, elegant flowers with buff to fawn-colored, purple-feathered exteriors that open to reveal a bright violet-purple interior, a striking two-tone effect unique among early crocus. It multiplies readily by offsets in gritty soil and is a valuable early nectar source, though flowers close on overcast days and open fully only in direct sun. Allow foliage to die back naturally before removing it to recharge the corm for next season.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to very early fall in well-drained, gritty soil; flowers emerge from bare ground within weeks of planting.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in late summer in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun. Native to Attica and southern Greece, this species is the wild ancestor from which cultivated saffron crocus (Crocus sativus) was selected, and it closely resembles its famous descendant, bearing pale lilac to white goblet flowers with prominent, long, deep-red stigmas in autumn ahead of the grassy foliage. Unlike the sterile triploid Crocus sativus, it sets viable seed and can spread naturally in a sunny, sharply drained bed such as a rock garden or gravel scree. The stigmas are edible and can be harvested as a saffron substitute, though yields are modest from garden-scale plantings.

planting.note: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep in late summer in well-drained soil; flowers emerge leafless from bare ground in autumn, with grassy foliage following in spring.

directions: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Native to the Pyrenees and northern Spain and long naturalized in parts of England, this species produces solitary, rich reddish-purple flowers directly from bare ground in early autumn, appearing well before the strap-like foliage, which emerges later and persists into spring. Unusually among crocus, it spreads by underground stolons as well as offsets and seed, allowing it to form dense, long-lived colonies once established in turf or a naturalistic border. As a true crocus it has three stamens and slender true leaves, distinguishing it from the toxic, superficially similar Colchicum.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this species flowers very early, often alongside snowdrops in late winter.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in a sunny, sharply drained spot such as a rock garden or scree bed, planting in fall for bloom in late winter to earliest spring. Native to the western Balkan mountains along the Dalmatian coast, it bears rounded, pale lilac to buff-lavender flowers with a soft yellow throat and faint bronze feathering on the outer petals, opening close to the ground on short stems. It multiplies readily by offsets in gritty, well-drained soil and is a reliable, long-lived rock garden subject once established. Allow the grassy foliage to die back naturally before removing it to recharge the corm for the following season.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this species blooms in early to mid spring.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in a sunny, sharply drained spot such as a rock garden or the front of a border, planting in fall for bloom in early to mid spring. Endemic to Corsica, it produces slender, pointed buds with purple-feathered, buff-colored exteriors that open in sunlight to reveal a rich reddish-violet interior with a bright orange throat, a striking contrast similar to its relative Crocus imperati. It multiplies slowly by offsets in gritty, well-drained soil and is best suited to a rock garden or alpine trough where drainage stays sharp through its summer dormancy. Flowers close on overcast days and open fully only in direct sun.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this species is among the earliest crocus to flower, opening in late winter to early spring.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in a sunny, sharply drained spot such as a rock garden or the front of a border, planting in fall for bloom in late winter to early spring. Native to a small area of Tuscany in central Italy, it bears soft lavender-blue flowers with a darker violet feathering at the base of the petals and a golden-yellow throat, opening wide in sunlight to reveal a subtly fragrant bloom. It multiplies readily by offsets in gritty, well-drained soil and naturalizes well in a sunny border or rock garden, making it a good introductory species for gardeners exploring species crocus beyond the common Dutch hybrids. Allow foliage to die back naturally before removing it to recharge the corm for next year.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this diminutive species blooms in mid spring, slightly later than the earliest species crocus.

directions: Set corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in a sunny, sharply drained spot such as an alpine trough or rock garden, planting in fall for bloom in mid spring. Endemic to Corsica and Sardinia, this is one of the smallest species crocus in cultivation, producing dainty purple flowers with a darker feathered exterior and a bright orange throat on very short stems close to the ground. It multiplies slowly by offsets in gritty, well-drained soil and is best suited to a rock garden, scree bed, or container where its diminutive scale will not be overwhelmed by larger neighbors. Flowers close on overcast days and open fully only in direct sun.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs in early to mid fall so they naturalize before the first hard freeze.

directions: Named for the Taurica (Crimean) region where this compact botanical form was collected, it brightens early spring woodland edges and lawns with the same vivid, nodding cobalt-blue bells as standard Siberian squill, but on noticeably shorter, tidier stems that make it especially well suited to rock gardens and small-scale plantings. Plant the small bulbs about three inches deep in humus-rich soil that stays moist in spring but can dry out somewhat once the foliage yellows in early summer. It tolerates being naturalized directly into turf, since its foliage matures and fades before regular mowing resumes, and it self-seeds readily to form drifts over the years. Leave seed capsules intact if you want colonies to spread naturally.
